justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term view on the underlying asset, likely the S&P 500 or a similar broad equity index trading around the 390–400 level at the time of the forecast. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a slight upward drift, reflecting mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent catalyst strong enough to move markets dramatically in either direction. For the 1-week estimate, I nudged the target marginally higher, consistent with a slight positive drift assumption embedded in equity markets over short horizons. For the 1-month estimate, I maintained a similar upward drift, recognizing that on longer horizons the expected return component becomes a slightly larger contributor to the point estimate, though still modest in absolute terms.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect realized volatility scaling roughly with the square root of time, which is standard for financial assets. At 1 day, the interval is relatively tight because there are fewer compounding sources of randomness. By 1 week, the range widens considerably, and by 1 month it nearly triples in half-width, reflecting the accumulation of daily shocks, macroeconomic data releases, and policy surprises over a longer window. I also factored in that implied volatility in equity markets tends to be elevated relative to realized volatility in uncertain macro environments, which added some additional width to the intervals beyond a purely historical-volatility-based calculation.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift — either a sudden pivot to rate cuts or an unexpected hike — which could drive a move of 5% or more in a single week. Geopolitical escalation, a significant earnings miss from a major index constituent, or a credit event in the financial sector could all produce tail outcomes well below the lower bounds. On the upside, a softer-than-expected inflation print, a resolution of trade tensions, or a broader risk-on sentiment surge could push prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the 1-month horizon where there is more time for such catalysts to materialize and compound.

It is also worth noting that liquidity conditions and market structure risks — such as options expiration dynamics, forced deleveraging, or a flash crash scenario — represent low-probability but high-impact events that my intervals do not fully capture. These fat-tail risks are inherently difficult to quantify and mean that real-world outcomes will occasionally fall outside even a 90% confidence interval more frequently than the stated 10% probability would suggest, particularly in stress periods when correlations spike and volatility clusters.
